package_info.why_malicious: Snake is a state-sponsored espionage malware developed by Russia’s FSB (Turla group) to covertly steal sensitive documents and maintain persistent, stealthy access to high-value targets worldwide. It forms a global peer-to-peer (P2P) network of compromised systems for long-term intelligence collection and is designed for advanced persistence, stealth, and anti-forensic capabilities.

execution_context.file_location: core Snake malware binary (varies by deployment)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Establishes encrypted peer-to-peer (P2P) communications with other infected hosts, relaying commands and exfiltrated data covertly.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (typical for Snake, but exact language not specified)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code establishes encrypted P2P connections with other infected systems, relays attacker commands and exfiltrated data between nodes, enabling covert global command and control and data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Encrypted P2P communications between compromised hosts are highly unusual for legitimate software and are a hallmark of advanced persistent threats, enabling covert command and control and data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not create covert, encrypted P2P networks for command and control or data exfiltration, especially without user awareness or legitimate business need.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some distributed computing or blockchain applications use P2P, but not for hidden, encrypted C2 or unauthorized data transfer between compromised hosts.
key_indicators: Encrypted P2P traffic to non-standard ports
Relay of attacker commands and exfiltrated data between hosts
No user-facing functionality or legitimate P2P purpose
Custom protocol handlers for covert network communication

execution_context.file_location: core Snake malware binary (varies by deployment)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Steals sensitive documents from infected systems and exfiltrates them via the P2P network.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (typical for Snake, but exact language not specified)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code scans the file system for sensitive documents, collects targeted files, and exfiltrates them through the encrypted P2P network to attacker-controlled nodes, resulting in covert data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated, covert collection and exfiltration of sensitive files is a core indicator of espionage malware, especially when performed without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not silently search for and transmit sensitive documents to unknown destinations without explicit user consent or legitimate business justification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or synchronization tools may access and transfer files, but only with user awareness, clear configuration, and to trusted, legitimate destinations.
key_indicators: Automated file system scanning for document types
Covert exfiltration of files via custom encrypted network protocol
No user notification or visible activity
Targeted collection of sensitive or high-value documents

execution_context.file_location: core Snake malware binary (varies by deployment)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Receives and executes self-destruct/overwrite commands, erasing its own vital components to disable itself.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (typical for Snake, but exact language not specified)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a specific remote command, the code overwrites its own executable components and deletes related files, effectively disabling the malware and removing forensic evidence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-destruct and anti-forensic capabilities are typical of advanced malware seeking to evade detection, hinder analysis, and prevent attribution by erasing itself on command.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not erase or overwrite itself in response to covert remote commands, especially in a manner designed to avoid forensic recovery.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate uninstallers remove software, but only in response to explicit user action and not via hidden network commands.
key_indicators: Remote-triggered self-deletion or overwriting of executables
Destruction of malware-related files and artifacts
Anti-forensic routines to hinder analysis and recovery
No user interaction or notification during self-destruction

attack_chain.action: Initial infection and installation of Snake malware on target systems.
Establishes encrypted P2P communications with other infected hosts, forming a global network.
Searches for and collects sensitive documents from infected systems.
Exfiltrates stolen data via the encrypted P2P network to attacker-controlled nodes.
On command (e.g., from FBI’s PEGASUS tool), Snake overwrites its own components to self-destruct and disable itself.

behavioral_signatures: Encrypted P2P network traffic between internal and external hosts using non-standard ports
Automated file system scanning and access to sensitive documents without user interaction
Remote-triggered self-deletion or overwriting of malware executables and artifacts
Absence of user-facing functionality despite persistent network and file activity
file_indicators: Unknown or suspicious binaries with persistence mechanisms (e.g., scheduled tasks, services, registry entries)
Unusual modification or deletion of malware-related files and executables
Presence of custom P2P protocol handler artifacts in binaries
Evidence of self-modifying or self-deleting code in executable sections
network_indicators: Non-standard encrypted traffic to multiple peer hosts, both internal and external
Unusual outbound connections to known Snake/Turla infrastructure or previously compromised hosts
Relay of data and commands between internal and external nodes using custom protocols
Absence of legitimate application-layer protocol signatures in encrypted traffic
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for encrypted P2P traffic patterns on non-standard ports, especially those relaying data between internal and external hosts; detect automated file system scanning and unauthorized access to sensitive documents; identify binaries with self-modifying or self-deleting capabilities and persistence mechanisms; correlate network connections and file artifacts with known Turla/Snake infrastructure and threat intelligence feeds; alert on remote-triggered self-destruction or anti-forensic routines.
